analysis.one_liner: Eliminates the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, the federal watchdog for consumer financial products.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or a vote and died in the House Financial Services Committee when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: This one-sentence bill would repeal the 2010 law that created the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB), the agency that writes and enforces rules for credit cards, mortgages, payday loans, debt collection, and credit reporting. With the bureau gone, no single federal agency would be responsible for policing those markets or returning money to consumers who were cheated. The bill was introduced by Rep. Byron Donalds with three original cosponsors, referred to the House Financial Services Committee, and never taken up before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Banks, credit card issuers, payday and installment lenders, debt collectors, and credit reporting agencies would benefit most. The CFPB is the main federal agency that sues these companies, issues fines, and forces refunds to consumers. Repealing its authorizing statute would eliminate that oversight and enforcement entirely.

how_it_helps.text: The bill repeals the Consumer Financial Protection Act of 2010 and revives the laws as they stood before the bureau existed, eliminating the CFPB as an agency.
Financial companies regulated by the CFPB would no longer face a dedicated agency that enforces rules against unfair, deceptive, or abusive practices in consumer credit markets.

analysis.who_pays: Consumers who use credit cards, take out mortgages, borrow from payday lenders, or deal with debt collectors and credit bureaus would pay by losing the federal agency charged with policing those markets and recovering money when companies break the rules.
analysis.who_pays_short: Ordinary users of credit and loans

drawbacks.text: Supporters of repeal argued the bureau was unaccountable: it is funded through the Federal Reserve rather than by congressional appropriations and is led by a single director, and critics claimed its rules raise the cost of offering credit, especially for smaller lenders.

Eliminating the bureau entirely, rather than reforming its funding or leadership, would leave no single agency responsible for consumer financial protection and would return markets like payday lending and debt collection to the patchwork of regulators that existed before 2010.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The cost to consumers clearly outweighs the benefit to industry. The stated aim — making the bureau more accountable to Congress — could have been pursued through narrower reforms to its funding or leadership; this bill instead removes consumer financial enforcement altogether, and its own terms restore pre-2010 law. The fact that it drew only a handful of cosponsors and never moved in committee suggests its sponsors knew the support was not there.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the House Financial Services Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never took it up, and it expired when the 118th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Byron Donalds introduced the Repeal CFPB Act on April 27, 2023, with Reps. Norman, McCormick, and Ogles as original cosponsors.
The same day, the bill was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services, and no further action was ever taken on it.
Nine Republicans cosponsored the bill; no Democrats did.
The bill died in committee when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, without a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Financial companies kept the consumer watchdog off their backs without needing to win a vote, since the bill never advanced. Consumers, meanwhile, kept existing CFPB protections only because the bill stalled — the effort to eliminate the bureau failed, but by inaction rather than decision.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Banks and lenders kept their watchdog

for.name: Rep. Byron Donalds
for.role: Sponsor, House Financial Services Committee member
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to eliminate the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau.

against.name: House Financial Services Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on April 27, 2023 and never scheduled it for consideration before the Congress ended.

against.name: House Democratic caucus
against.what_they_did: None of the 216 House Democrats cosponsored the bill, and no Democratic member supported it in the record.

sides.party_line_note: All 10 listed supporters were Republicans (the sponsor plus 9 Republican cosponsors); no Democrat cosponsored or acted for the bill.

industries.note: Repeal would free these companies from the CFPB's rulemaking, exams, fines, and consumer refunds in credit card and mortgage markets. Consumers would lose the agency that polices those same markets, so the industry's gain is the public's loss.

The CFPB has been the primary federal regulator targeting lending practices that trap borrowers in cycles of debt. Eliminating it would leave these lenders with far less federal oversight of a core business model.
The CFPB writes and enforces the main federal rules on debt collection conduct. Repeal would return oversight to a weaker pre-2010 patchwork.
The bureau regulates credit bureaus' handling of consumer data and disputes. Repeal would remove its dedicated supervision of the firms that control consumers' credit files.
